shots.text: Every morning, before eight, someone decides which aircraft will fly.
That decision should rest on everything the fleet already knows.
Health data. Technical records. Spares. Work in progress.
Phalanx Twin brings it together — and turns it into decisions.
The problem statement is blunt. Availability is low because maintenance is reactive — and the data that could prevent it isn't integrated.
Audits keep finding the same thing: aircraft are lost to waiting — for parts, for repair, for a decision.
In our fleet, one aircraft has been on the ground for eighty days, waiting for a brake chute — a consumable whose demand simply follows landings.
Another has had its hydraulic pump removed twenty-eight times for one alarm. Every pump the shop tested came back: no fault found.
Nearly twelve hundred alerts this season. More prediction alone would only add more.
And any answer must be explainable, honest about time — and run fully offline.
Phalanx Twin is a decision-support digital twin for the flight line.
It answers four questions: what's happening, why, what happens next — and what we should do.
Everything starts from one frozen data contract. A release gate admits it, and an as-of store guarantees we only use what was known at the time.
If a record wasn't ingested by six, no model, rule or order can use it.
That builds one state: a belief about every aircraft and every serialised part — with its uncertainty.

Engines read that state. We chose models that fit sparse, censored maintenance data — calibrated classifiers, Bayesian isolation, survival models — and kept time-series foundation models as baselines, not decision-makers.
Triage turns twelve hundred alerts into seven decisions.
Versioned policies and optimisers propose orders, simulation tests them against the status quo, a person approves — and every step lands on one tamper-evident log.
Monday, 06:00. Six of eight aircraft are mission capable.
shots.spoken: Monday morning, six o'clock. Six of eight aircraft are mission capable.

shots.text: This season, most of the waiting came from tyres and brake chutes — demand you can predict from the flying plan.
Today's board has seven issues — each with the evidence and the score behind it.
TJ107. The system doesn't say replace the pump. It says stop — and shows why.
shots.spoken: T J one oh seven. The system doesn't say, replace the pump. It says stop — and shows why.

shots.text: In the twin, the alarm's reporter and its suspects light up where they sit in the aircraft.
It stayed with this aircraft through ten different pumps. The evidence follows the tail — not the part.
Learned from outcomes, the chance this pump is actually faulty is half a percent. Remove it again, and it's ninety-eight percent likely to come back 'no fault found'.
So it recommends the test that resolves the most uncertainty per man-hour.
Every recommendation comes from a rule you can read. Hard limits live in code; anything airworthiness-sensitive waits for a human signature.
Before it reaches the board, each order is tested on paired simulations of the same futures — our plan against the status quo.
For parts, a warning only helps if it beats the lead time — and the fork gate drops orders, like early tyres, that change nothing.
At 07:45 the board freezes. At 08:00, orders go out — each one cited, signed where it must be, and safe to retry.
shots.spoken: At seven forty-five the board freezes. At eight, orders go out — each one cited, signed where it must be, and safe to retry.

shots.text: Ask why any order was issued, and the chain answers — from data release to signature.
All of this runs live on IBM LinuxONE: the simulator, models, rules, daily loop and audit log — on one mainframe-class server.
shots.spoken: All of this runs live on IBM Linux One: the simulator, models, rules, daily loop and audit log — on one mainframe-class server.

shots.text: Rebuilt there, it reproduces every record, row for row — and simulates a day for all eight aircraft in three and a half seconds.
IBM Z is built for exactly this: availability, hardware-protected keys, confidential computing and AI on the chip — real-time AI for critical decisions.
Outcomes become labels, and models and rules are promoted only through gates.
Today, one question means five places: the tech log, the BIT downloads, the parts ledger, the shop reports and the plan.
Here, you just ask. The assistant plans, then reads only what it needs — as of 06:00 — through read-only tools.
shots.spoken: Here, you just ask. The assistant plans, then reads only what it needs — as of six a.m. — through read-only tools.

shots.text: Every number in its answer comes from a tool, never from the model, and every claim cites its records — even the what-if, from the same paired simulations the board uses.
It runs on one air-gapped box, first words in about a second — and it can only draft. The signature stays with the officer.
On thirty paired simulations, the TJ107 decision adds twenty-two points of mission-capable time next month — and saves a hundred and sixteen man-hours.

shots.text: Phalanx Twin. One state. One loop. One log.
